analysis.one_liner: Caps prescription drug prices in federal health programs at prices paid in other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, no committee action, and no vote; it was referred to committee six weeks before the 115th Congress ended and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to set a yearly maximum price for every prescription drug, based on the median price charged in eleven other developed countries like Japan, Germany, and Canada. That cap would apply to Medicare, Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, TRICARE, Veterans Affairs care, federal employees' coverage, and Indian Health Service programs. It would also require drug manufacturers to offer those same capped prices to uninsured and privately insured people nationwide.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of millions of people covered by Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA health care, federal employees' insurance, and Indian Health Service programs, plus uninsured and privately insured Americans, who under the bill's terms would all be entitled to the capped reference price.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors, veterans, Medicaid and CHIP enrollees

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs HHS to set an annual reference price for each prescription drug equal to the median price charged for that drug in eleven reference countries, and caps what federal health programs pay at that price, including cost-sharing.
The cap covers Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA health care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian Health Service programs, reaching a very large share of American patients.

As a condition for reimbursement under federal programs, manufacturers must offer drugs at the reference price to all individuals, including the uninsured and people with private coverage, extending the price cap beyond the federal programs themselves.
The cap counts any manufacturer discounts or rebates toward the price, and applies to both brand-name and generic drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose US prices would be pulled down to the median price charged in Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden; drug spending currently drives prices well above that level.

drawbacks.text: The reference price is set as the median foreign price, so US prices would fall to the middle of other developed countries' prices; if enforcement is looser abroad than in the US, that method could push some prices below levels those systems actually achieve.

Capping revenue at foreign median prices would reduce expected returns on drugs sold in the US, the world's most profitable market, which drug makers argue would slow investment in new medicines; the bill contains no offsetting research incentive.

The bill applies the cap to the total acquisition cost including rebates, which could disrupt the existing rebate-based negotiations between manufacturers, insurers, and pharmacy benefit managers without a transition plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would directly cut the price Americans pay for prescription drugs across nearly every public program and extend those prices to the private market, a large tangible gain for patients and taxpayers. The honest cost is to pharmaceutical companies' US revenues and possibly to the pace of new drug development, a trade-off the bill makes without any offset for innovation.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Merkley introduced the bill in late November 2018, weeks before the Congress ended, it was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee with no cosponsors, and no committee or floor action ever followed before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced S. 3680, the Low Drug Prices Act, on November 29, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No cosponsors joined the bill, and the HELP Committee never took it up; the action history shows no further steps after the referral.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and all bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they continue to charge US prices well above the median prices in other developed countries for Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs, and patients continue to bear those higher costs. Congressional leadership and the committee are also spared a fight over drug pricing.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 29, 2018, to cap federal-program drug prices at the median price in eleven other developed countries.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sole sponsor was a Democrat with no cosponsors from either party, so the bill's level of party support was never tested.

industries.note: The bill caps what these companies can charge federal programs and, by extension, all US buyers at the median price charged in eleven other developed countries, directly cutting their US revenue on Medicare, Medicaid, and private-market sales. Their current higher US prices are the profit source the bill removes.

Capping acquisition costs including rebates would cut what insurers and pharmacy benefit managers pay for drugs, but it would also collapse the rebate leverage that is central to how pharmacy benefit managers make money, restructuring their role rather than simply helping or hurting them.

The reference price applies to generics as well as brand-name drugs, but generics are generally already priced well below foreign medians in the US, so the practical effect on them is smaller than on brand-name manufacturers.
